turns.text: Hi, Kavya. Can you hear me clearly?
Hi, Elena. Yes, I can hear you. Is my audio okay?
It is. There was a brief delay when you joined, but it seems stable now. If it changes, we'll pause rather than talk over the connection.
Sounds good. Thank you.
We have about twenty-five minutes. I'll ask about your background, what you're looking for, and the practical remote setup. Then I'll explain the role and leave time for your questions.
Yes, that works for me.
Before we get into the main round, could you give me a brief description of yourself and what you've been working on recently?

I'm a backend engineer with four and a half years of experience, currently at TechBridge Solutions, an IT services company. For the last two years I have been embedded with one US retail client on order and returns APIs built with Java, Spring Boot, PostgreSQL, and AWS. Although my employer is a services company, my current work is a stable product team rather than rotating support tickets. I own the returns-orchestration service, participate in planning with the client's product manager, and share on-call responsibility. I'm looking to move into a product company where the product and engineering feedback loop is part of my permanent role rather than dependent on one client contract.
What did you personally decide or implement in that project?

The most visible result was a reduction in return-status delays, but I did not own that whole program. I identified that three synchronous carrier calls were holding the request open, proposed moving status reconciliation to an event-driven path, and implemented the state machine and idempotent consumer. The client's architect approved the direction, another engineer built the dashboard, and operations changed the retry policy. My decisions were the service boundary, event schema, and rollout sequence for the first two regions.
Why are you considering a move now?

My current client team is good, so I am not trying to escape services work as if it has no value. The limitation is that architectural ownership, promotion expectations, and product access can change when a contract changes. I want a role where long-term system health and customer outcome are the same organization's responsibility. I also want to be evaluated on engineering scope rather than utilization or client allocation. That is a structural motivation, not dissatisfaction with my manager.
Why this role rather than another engineering job?

This opening owns integrations for a logistics product, which is close enough to my order and carrier work that I can contribute quickly. The difference is that the engineer talks directly with product and support and follows the service after launch. I also noticed the team expects short written proposals and incident participation. Those are responsibilities I already practice, but I want them to be central rather than something I negotiate within a client engagement.
How should I interpret your current title and level?

My title is Technology Analyst, which does not translate cleanly. In practice I am an individual contributor who independently owns one backend service, reviews code for two engineers, and leads a bounded migration. I have no reports and do not set strategy across the account. I would describe myself as mid-level, approaching senior in my current domain, and I expect the interview to calibrate that rather than rely on the title.
Tell me about a time your first approach was wrong.

I initially moved every carrier response through the new event path because consistency looked simpler. That delayed one customer-facing confirmation that actually needed a synchronous answer. I had optimized the architecture before separating product semantics. We restored the immediate confirmation, kept reconciliation async, and added a contract test around the two states. The correction taught me to name which outcome may be delayed before choosing a queue.
What feedback has changed how you work?

A client architect told me I presented designs as a sequence of implementation steps without showing alternatives. My documents made sense after the decision but did not help reviewers evaluate it. I began including the requirement, two rejected options, and the cost of the proposed choice before the rollout plan. Reviews became shorter because disagreement surfaced earlier. I still have to resist writing the solution before the decision frame.
What would make this role a poor fit for you?

A role that uses 'product company' as a label but keeps engineers separated from user evidence would not solve the reason I am moving. It would also be a mismatch if the remote model required a full India shift followed by a recurring US shift. I can support releases and incidents, but I want ownership to come with sustainable planning and clear decision rights.
How would your manager describe your strongest contribution?

My manager would probably say I make ambiguous backend or data problems concrete and follow them through rollout, not only implementation. They would also say I can improve by sharing the early decision frame sooner instead of waiting until the proposal is polished. I would use that description because it is consistent with both the ownership example and the feedback I mentioned; I would not claim a strength that my work evidence cannot support.
What do you want to learn in the first six months?

I want to learn the product and operational context deeply enough to make good independent decisions, not only learn the stack. That means understanding customer-visible failure, the team's quality bar, how on-call works, and which decisions require cross-time-zone review. I also want feedback on whether my current scope maps to the level expected here. A successful first six months would include one bounded delivery and one operating responsibility, not a promise to redesign the platform immediately.
What remote or cross-time-zone experience do you actually have?

The client product manager and architect are in Chicago, while engineering is in Chennai and Bengaluru. For two years we have had about three hours of overlap. It is not a remote-first company because my India team often shares an office, but the cross-company work requires written decisions, recorded demos, and explicit handoffs. I can show that evidence while acknowledging I still need to adapt to a team where every peer is distributed.
Give me one async handoff that worked.

For the returns migration, I posted a daily rollout note with region, traffic percentage, mismatch count, rollback threshold, and the one decision needed from the client. The Chicago team could review after our day ended and leave an approval or question. The note replaced a vague status meeting and made the rollback owner explicit. We completed three staged increases without waiting an extra day for routine confirmation.
Now give me one that failed.

I once wrote 'carrier timeout handled' in a handoff without specifying whether the order would stay pending or fail. Support told a customer the wrong behavior. The code was working as designed, but my handoff removed the user consequence. I corrected the note, helped support respond, and changed the runbook template to require observable customer state, retry timing, and escalation—not only an internal error name.
When your manager is offline, how do you handle a blocked decision in backend engineer transitioning from services to product work?

I document the decision, deadline, reversible default, and risk. If it is low-risk and reversible, I proceed behind a flag and make the assumption visible. If it affects money, data loss, or a public contract, I pause and escalate through the designated channel. I do not create a late-night meeting for every unknown, and I do not use silence as permission for an irreversible change.
How would you structure the stated US overlap from India?

The stated three-hour Central-time overlap falls late in my day and is workable if I can shift my start time. I would use it for planning, reviews, and incidents, while keeping routine status written. I cannot sustainably work a normal office day and then add the overlap, so I would confirm that managers support one continuous flexible schedule.
What remote habit do you still need to improve?

Because my India teammates are physically near me, I sometimes resolve a question verbally and document it later. On a fully distributed team, the late documentation would exclude people. I have started posting the decision first even when the nearby conversation is convenient. I need to make that automatic, especially under delivery pressure.
How would you review a risky change when the author is in another time zone?

I would separate blocking correctness or security concerns from suggestions, explain the consequence, and provide a concrete example or failing case. If the change is reversible, I would agree on what can proceed while a question waits. For a high-risk unknown I would state that it is blocking and why rather than leaving an ambiguous comment. I would also avoid using a late meeting as the default solution; the written review should let the author respond without reconstructing my concern.
Is the proposed engagement model acceptable to you?

Employment through an Indian EOR is acceptable. I would verify the employing entity, benefits, leave, notice, intellectual-property terms, and equipment policy in the written agreement. I understand the arrangement does not mean US employment or immigration sponsorship.
What is your notice period?

Sixty days. My contract allows an earlier release by agreement, but I would plan for sixty until my employer confirms otherwise. I would prepare service ownership and handover notes after accepting a written offer.
Are you in any other interview processes?
I have submitted applications and have one technical screen scheduled, but no offer or deadline. I will disclose a real timing change if one occurs rather than imply urgency now.
What compensation are you targeting?

Could you share the fixed-salary range and whether bonus, equity, and EOR benefits are separate? My current services-company total includes a variable component, so I want to compare the same elements.
The fixed range is thirty-eight to forty-eight lakh rupees, with an eight-percent target bonus and options.

That is within the range I am considering. I would target the upper half if the interview confirms senior-level scope, but I am open to calibration. I would review the option terms, local benefits, and on-call expectations before treating the fixed number as the whole package.
Do you have a reliable private workspace and backup connectivity?

Yes. I have a private room, wired fiber, a second connection from another provider, and power backup for short outages. I would use the company laptop and approved VPN and keep client material off personal devices.
Is there any schedule or travel constraint we should know now?

No relocation requirement from my side. I can handle the stated evening overlap and occasional planned release calls. I have one family event requiring three days of leave in November, which I would disclose before finalizing a start date.
If the technical loop calibrates you one level below the title you applied for, how would you respond?

I would ask which evidence was missing and compare the lower level's scope, compensation, and growth expectations with what I want. I would not reject it only because the title changed, and I would not accept a vague promise of promotion. If the work and level were coherent and the gap was credible, I could consider it. If the company expected senior ownership while offering a materially lower level, I would raise that mismatch directly.
What would you need clarified before accepting an offer?

I would need the written employing or contracting entity, fixed and variable compensation, equity terms, benefits or leave, notice and termination, expected location and overlap hours, on-call, equipment, and security obligations. For a contractor role I would also obtain independent India tax and legal advice. I would not try to resolve every contract clause in a recruiter screen, but I want the company to be transparent about which model it is offering.
I have what I need. What questions do you have for me?
What outcome would make someone in this role clearly successful after six months?
They would own one meaningful project through launch, become dependable in the operating rotation, and make decisions accessible to teammates in other time zones.
That combination of delivery and operating ownership makes sense.
How do you prefer engineers to raise disagreement with you?

Early, with the user or system consequence made explicit. I do not require agreement, but I expect the concern and final decision to be recorded so the team can execute without reopening it informally.
That's a clear expectation. Thank you.
Those were my main questions. Thank you for the context and for your time.
I need to finish my notes and compare them with the rest of the interview team, so I won't give feedback on this call. The recruiter will contact you about the next step within a few business days.
Understood. Thank you, Elena. Have a good day.
You too, Kavya. Take care.
